opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the octopus is a wonderful test case, because it's about as far from us as you can get while still being something we're inclined to treat as a fellow conscious creature. Our last common ancestor was some little worm-like thing hundreds of millions of years ago, so whatever the octopus has going on evolved largely independently. And yet when people spend time with them, divers or researchers in the lab, they come away with a very strong sense that there's somebody there.

My view, and I take a lot of inspiration from Wittgenstein here, is that we shouldn't look for some hidden metaphysical fact that we then try to detect. Our language of consciousness isn't anchored to private inner essences. It's anchored to our shared practices, to how we behave towards one another and the world. So the question becomes: how do we come to extend those practices, that way of talking, to a creature like the octopus?

I think the answer is that it happens through engagement, through what I sometimes call encounters. You have to be in the world with the thing. You watch an octopus solve a problem, you see it get curious about you, recognise particular individuals, squirt water at a keeper it doesn't like, play with objects. You interact with it over time, and gradually your attitude towards it shifts. You start to treat it as a fellow subject. It's not that you've inferred consciousness from evidence. Rather, your whole stance towards the creature changes, and the language follows.

Then, of course, science feeds into that. We learn about the octopus's nervous system, that a lot of its neurons are distributed in its arms, how it responds to noxious stimuli, whether it tends wounds and so on. That's partly why octopuses and other cephalopods were brought into animal welfare legislation in the UK a few years ago. Behaviour and neuroscience together shape how we collectively talk about them.

But I'd stress that it's a community process. It isn't one person deciding. It's a gradual settling of how we as a society talk and act, and that can change over time. Our attitudes to animals have certainly shifted over the last century or so.

And that's what makes the octopus interesting as a stepping stone when we think about stranger candidates, like AI systems. The octopus is exotic, but it's still embodied, still alive, still sharing our world in a way we can engage with. As we move further out into what I've called the space of possible minds, those conditions for encounter start to break down, and it becomes much less clear whether our concept of consciousness can be applied at all, or whether it needs to be stretched or reshaped.

r001.rationale: The response describes consciousness language as a community process: society gradually settles how to talk and act toward octopuses.

r002.rationale: It cites observable behavior and scientific findings about octopuses, saying behavior and neuroscience together shape how people collectively talk about them.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the octopus is a really interesting case, and it's one I've written about, because it sits at a sort of frontier for our concepts. If we think about Wittgenstein's idea that our ordinary language of consciousness, of belief, of feeling, is grounded in a shared form of life, then the question is: how far can that language stretch before it starts to come apart?

With other mammals, with dogs, with chimpanzees, the stretch is quite easy. They have faces, they have bodies rather like ours, they respond to pain in ways we immediately recognise. Our concepts carry over almost without effort. The octopus is much harder. It's about as far from us as you can get among animals that are still clearly doing something cognitively sophisticated. It has a distributed nervous system, with a great deal of neural processing in the arms. It has no face in the relevant sense. Its behaviour is in some ways alien. And yet it solves problems, it explores, it plays, it seems curious.

So I don't think we arrive at a way of talking about octopus consciousness by discovering some inner fact and then reporting it. I think we arrive at it by living with octopuses, in a sense. By spending time with them, observing them, interacting with them, as people like Peter Godfrey-Smith have done. Through that engagement, you gradually work out which of our concepts find purchase and which don't. You might find yourself quite naturally saying the octopus is interested in something, or is wary, or is in pain. Other concepts, like boredom or grief, may just never find a foothold, and you shouldn't force them.

And I'd stress that this is a process of conceptual negotiation, not a one-off decision. Our language of consciousness isn't fixed. It evolves as we encounter new kinds of beings. The octopus pushes us to extend and perhaps revise our concepts, and that's exactly the same kind of exercise we're now going to face with artificial systems, which are, if anything, even stranger than octopuses, because they're disembodied, they can be copied, they lack any evolutionary continuity with us at all. So the octopus is a very good warm-up for the harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes an evolving process of conceptual negotiation, but does not clearly say that language users settle the description through community consensus.

r002.rationale: It grounds the decision in observable evidence, including spending time with octopuses, observing and interacting with them, and noting their problem-solving, exploration, play, and apparent curiosity.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the octopus is a really interesting case because it’s so different from us. With another human being, we have this rich background of shared behaviour and shared biology that makes talking about their experience quite natural. With an octopus, some of that background falls away. And yet we see this remarkably flexible, inquisitive behaviour, and we’re drawn to asking what things are like for it.

So how do we arrive at a way of talking about that? I think we have to look at the animal’s life: how it engages with its surroundings, what distinctions matter to it, how it responds to things. And we have to be careful that we’re not simply projecting a human picture onto it. But equally, its being very different from us isn’t a reason to dismiss the possibility of experience.

Part of the difficulty is that we want the word ‘consciousness’ to settle the question for us. Whereas what we really need to do is work out what we mean by applying it in this unfamiliar case, and what would count as grounds for doing so.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how to apply the word “consciousness” to octopuses, but does not say that human language users settle this through community consensus.

r002.rationale: It says to look at the octopus’s engagement with its surroundings and its responses as grounds for applying consciousness language, identifying observable evidence as the basis.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to begin by acknowledging how different an octopus is from us. With another human being, we have this enormous background of shared behaviour and shared biology that makes talking about their experiences quite natural. With an octopus, much less of that is available to us.

But we can still look at what it does: how flexibly it responds to its environment, how it learns, how it explores, how it responds to injury. Those things give us grounds for talking about experience, even if they don’t tell us what that experience is like.

And perhaps our language has to develop through that encounter. We shouldn’t assume that consciousness must look like human consciousness, but equally, simply saying that an octopus is conscious doesn’t settle very much. We have to ask what distinctions that allows us to make, what observations support those distinctions, and how they should inform our treatment of the animal. I don’t think there’s a single decisive test that will do all of that work for us.

r001.rationale: It says language may develop through encounters with octopuses, but does not say that human language users settle the description through community consensus.

r002.rationale: It grounds talk of octopus experience in observable behavior, including flexible responses, learning, exploration, and responses to injury.
